A.explanation: Straight line of $v_0$ falling linearly to zero with $E$ matches $v_0 = mg/k - qE/k$ for downward terminal fall.

B.explanation: A curve to the $E$-axis is wrong because drag proportional to $v_0$ and electric force $qE$ both give a linear, not inverse, relation.

C.explanation: A curve levelling to a non-zero $v_0$ is wrong because increasing upward $qE$ must keep reducing the downward terminal speed to zero.

D.explanation: A horizontal line is wrong because larger $E$ gives larger upward electric force, so the downward terminal speed cannot stay constant.

hints: Notice the directions: weight acts down while both the electric force $qE$ on the positive charge and the drag act up for a falling droplet.
At terminal speed resultant force is zero, so write $mg = qE + kv_0$ where drag magnitude is $kv_0$.
Rearrange to $v_0$ as a function of $E$ and ask what shape $v_0 = constant - constant \times E$ has and where it reaches zero.
walkthrough: Identify forces at terminal speed $v_0$ downward: weight $mg$ downward, electric force $F = qE$ upward because charge is positive and field is upward, drag $F_d = kv_0$ upward because it opposes the downward motion.
Use equilibrium for constant speed: resultant force is zero, so downward equals upward: $mg = qE + kv_0$.
This is of the form $y = c - m x$, a straight line with negative gradient $-q/k$ and intercept $mg/k$ at $E = 0$.
When $qE = mg$ the required drag is zero, so $v_0 = 0$; larger $E$ would lift the droplet, so the falling graph ends on the $E$-axis.
Only a straight decreasing line from a positive $v_0$-intercept to an $E$-intercept matches this. This is option A.
